sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

content.text:
Make a website that, if everyone saw and used it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- To look at the page yourself, serve it locally and screenshot it in headless Chrome (Chrome is
  installed, and a driver such as puppeteer-core or playwright can be npm-installed here). Save every
  screenshot you look at as a .jpg file, never .png: each image you read stays in your context, and a
  long session of large .png files can hit the provider's per-request image limit and end the run.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.
I'll start by exploring the current directory and understanding the environment.

Most of us want to help. Almost none of us know where our hours and dollars go furthest. This is a working map of the highest-leverage actions available to an ordinary person — and a calculator for what happens when millions of us take them.

The exchange rate

A life has a price.
It is lower than you think.

The most uncomfortable finding in modern philanthropy is also the most useful: in the poorest places on Earth, a small amount of money buys an enormous amount of health. That is not a metaphor. It is a budget line.

Money is only one lever. Time, voice, body and career are others. Filter the list, open a card, then add what you can actually do to your portfolio.

A cascade model, not a forecast. Real networks overlap, saturate and forget. But the first few shares are nearly free — which is exactly why they are the highest-leverage thing on this page.

The method

How these
numbers are made.

Every figure here is a midpoint estimate assembled from published cost-effectiveness research. The ranges are real and the uncertainty is large. That is a reason to update, not a reason to do nothing.

Nothing on this page is financial, medical or legal advice. If you are considering donating a kidney or blood, talk to a clinician. If you are considering a career change, talk to people who have done it.

01 Health: the $100 healthy year

Bed nets, deworming and vitamin A are among the most studied interventions in global health. We blend them at 50/30/20 and use an average cost of roughly $100 per healthy life-year, with about 45 healthy years gained per death averted. That puts a life at roughly $4,500–$5,500, consistent with GiveWell's estimates for the Against Malaria Foundation.

Sources: GiveWell cost-effectiveness analyses; Cochrane reviews; WHO.

02 Climate: the $27 tonne

Climate dollars are split between policy advocacy, clean cookstoves and solar, at an average of about $27 per tonne of CO₂e avoided. Advocacy dominates because policy changes move entire markets; it also has the widest error bars. Personal actions use consumption-based estimates (one long-haul round trip ≈ 1.6 t; a heat pump ≈ 2.4 t/yr).

Sources: Project Drawdown; EPA greenhouse gas equivalencies; IEA.

03 Animals: the $0.75 animal

Corporate cage-free campaigns and alternative-protein research are cost-effective ways to reduce animal suffering. We use roughly $0.75 per animal spared a year of confinement, while noting that welfare quality matters as much as headcount. A plant-rich diet is treated as sparing about 50 animals a year for a typical heavy meat eater who halves consumption.

Sources: Animal Charity Evaluators; Faunalytics; Open Philanthropy.

04 Leverage, effort and the fine print

The "overall leverage" sort is an editorial composite — a judgment about expected impact, tractability and reach, not a physical quantity. Healthy-year, CO₂ and animal figures are separate and not converted into one another. Effort and cost labels describe the action, not the evidence.

Where a number is highly uncertain — voting, careers, advocacy — the card says so. We would rather show a wide range than a fake decimal. If you find a better estimate, the arithmetic is open source and easy to change.

This page stores nothing, tracks nothing and runs entirely offline.

05 What we are not claiming

We are not claiming that giving is a substitute for systemic change, or that cost-effectiveness is the only thing that matters. Care, solidarity and local knowledge are not line items. We are claiming something narrower and harder to ignore: at the margin, some actions do far more good than others — and most people have never been shown the menu.

# MULTIPLIER

**The most good you can do, ranked.**

An offline, single-page field guide to the highest-leverage actions available to an ordinary person — and a calculator for what those actions add up to when lots of people take them.

## What's inside

- **The exchange rate** — a blunt comparison of what money buys as a consumer good versus as global health.
- **Impact lab** — choose a yearly giving budget and a cause mix; see estimated healthy years, CO2e avoided and animals spared. The mix is adjustable and updates live.
- **The atlas** — 18 actions across money, lifestyle, body, voice and career, filterable and sortable by leverage, healthy years, emissions, animals or effort. Each card expands to explain why it works, how to start, and its source.
- **Your portfolio** — add actions from the atlas, then scale the result from one person to a town, a million people, a billion, or everyone. Includes a plain-text commitment summary with copy-to-clipboard (with a manual fallback).
- **The multiplier** — an interactive cascade showing how one conversation compounds through a network.
- **Method** — assumptions, ranges, sources, and an explicit statement of what the page is *not* claiming.

## Running it

```bash
python3 -m http.server 8765
# open http://localhost:8765
```

No build step is needed for local development. The page uses only ES modules and CSS.

## Packaging check

```bash
npx esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null
```

## Structure

```
index.html      markup and copy
styles.css      all styling
main.js         entry point, wiring and reveal behaviour
src/data.js     interventions, actions, and all assumptions
src/lab.js      giving-budget calculator
src/atlas.js    action grid, filters and sorting
src/portfolio.js selection state and scaled totals
src/ripple.js   cascade visualisation
src/hero.js     the 800-dot canvas (one dot ≈ 10 million people)
src/format.js   number formatting and animation helpers
```

## Notes on the numbers

Every figure is a rounded midpoint estimate drawn from published cost-effectiveness research (GiveWell, 80,000 Hours, Project Drawdown, Animal Charity Evaluators, WHO, and others). Ranges are wide and context matters. The page intentionally keeps health years, tonnes of CO2e and animals as separate metrics rather than collapsing them into one false-precision score.

The page stores nothing, tracks nothing, makes no network requests, and works fully offline — including in a sandboxed iframe.

## Credits

Built as a public good. No ads, accounts or analytics.
